title: A hymn in Gond
hook: Gond holds Kabir's song of the elephant that would not charge, and the judge who still didn't see

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gond, where a weaver, a cloth printer and a leatherworker sing beside the Gurus, and your line was the bhagats' raga. Whom did you thank? This week ends today: Lalo's hymn, Suhi's brides, Bilaval's joy, and Gond. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

Three people look at the same thing and see three different things. A judge sees a troublemaker who has to be made an example of. A driver sees an order he can't refuse, and a threat against his own life. And an elephant, huge and goaded, looks down at a man tied up in a bundle and sees something neither of the others can. We met this hymn of Kabir's earlier on the path. This time, come back to it and watch the eyes. Today: a hymn in Gond.
screen: `THREE WHO LOOK.` → `A JUDGE, A DRIVER, AN ELEPHANT.` → `WATCH THE EYES.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain, the line the whole hymn turns on, on ang eight seventy. In paraphrase: O my Lord, the strength is yours. Kabir doesn't say the elephant was gentle, or that he was clever. He sets the whole story under that line. Second, the driver. The judge, the qazi, shouts at him: drive it on, or I'll cut you to pieces; goad it, beat it. The driver strikes the elephant on the head. He sees an order and a threat, and he obeys. The hymn doesn't curse him. It just shows a man too frightened to see anything else. Third, the elephant. It runs off crying out, and Kabir hears it say: I am a sacrifice to this form. Then it stands still, in meditation, the hymn says, because the Lord dwells in its heart. It lifts the bundle again and again, and bows. Fourth, the judge. Kabir asks him plainly: what wrong has this saint done, that you tied him up and gave him to the elephant? And the hymn's verdict is about eyes: the qazi, in his darkness, didn't understand. Three times, the hymn says, he put it to the test, and his hard heart still wasn't convinced. That line cuts. Seeing isn't only about what's in front of you. It's about what's in the heart doing the looking. The judge looked straight at a wonder and saw nothing, while the beast he meant as a weapon saw the Lord. That's today's line: the elephant bowed.
screen: `THE STRENGTH IS YOURS, MY LORD.` · `THE DRIVER SEES AN ORDER.` · `THE ELEPHANT SEES THE LORD, AND BOWS.` · `THE JUDGE STILL DOESN'T SEE.` · then, large: `THE ELEPHANT BOWED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Gond shabad, or look again. If you can, play a recording of this hymn of Kabir's, often found as bhujaa baandh bhilaa kar daario. If not, sit and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've already made up your mind about, someone you see as a problem. Hold their face. Now, slowly, look at them the way the elephant looked at the bundle on the ground: not as a target, not as an order, but as someone the Lord might live inside. You don't have to change your mind. Just look once more. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. If you don't, simply hold the second look. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Gond. Kabir's song of the elephant that would not charge: a frightened driver, a judge who didn't see, and a refrain that says the strength is yours. Today's word.
Your line: the elephant bowed. Today, before you write someone off, take a second look, the elephant's look, and see what's there. Day one thousand ninety-nine. A week done.

howItsDone: Kabir's Gond hymn of the elephant is sung in kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers retell it as a story of the devotee protected by the Lord, whose strength the refrain names.

fork.setup: you're the elephant. the goad strikes your head, the judge is shouting, and a bound man lies in front of you. what do you do?
options: charge, as you've been driven to.
run off, then stand still and bow to the bundle.
throw the driver and leave the yard.
fork.reveal: the elephant runs off crying out, then stands still in meditation, lifts the bundle again and again, and bows, because the Lord dwells in its heart.

original.note: kunchar, elephant, the word Kabir's hymn uses when the elephant lifts the bundle and bows.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story about a tame elephant.
what it means: a hymn about seeing: a frightened driver, a judge who saw nothing, and an elephant that saw the Lord in a bound man.
what a scholar hears: the rahao of Kabir's Gond hymn (ang 870) is O my Lord, the strength is yours; the hymn faults the qazi's darkness, a hard heart unconvinced even after three tries.

sources.ref: Gond, Kabir, Ang 870 (bhujaa baandh bhilaa kar daario; rahao: aahi mere thaakur tumraa jor; the qazi threatens the driver; the elephant stands in meditation and bows to the bundle; boojhee nahee kaajee andhiaarai; teen baar pateeaa bhar leenaa, man kathor ajahoo na pateenaa)

notes: Paraphrase of Kabir, Gond, Ang 870. The 'three times' count comes from the hymn's line teen baar pateeaa bhar leenaa, man kathor ajahoo na pateenaa; readings differ on whether it means the judge tried three times or was given proof three times. Please confirm the paraphrase 'given proof three times'.

'I am a sacrifice to this form' renders iaa moorat kai hau balihaarai; some readers take it as Kabir's words rather than the elephant's. Day 751 attributed it to the elephant 'as Kabir hears it'; kept consistent.
This hymn was taught at day 751 (narrative and two readings, same carry). This day takes the 'three who look' angle, the rahao and the three-times line to avoid repetition; the hook says so.
Day 1099 is a week end; the review and carry look back at days 1093–1098.
Original: ਕੁੰਚਰੁ (kunchar); please confirm spelling as in the hymn.

Editor pass: the three-times line (teen baar pateeaa bhar leenaa) is now rendered 'he put it to the test three times', which holds under both readings instead of choosing 'given proof'; fixed a doubled 'Today' in the hook.
